title: Row multiplication and duplicate detection
objective: Predict how many rows a join returns from the grain of each table, detect fan-out and duplicate rows, and fix inflated aggregates by pre-aggregating before joining.
context: Finance noticed that a dashboard reported customer 7's revenue as 22,189.76 when their real gross revenue is 1,305.28. Nobody wrote a wrong formula — a join multiplied the rows. This lesson is about knowing the grain of every table and checking COUNT(*) before and after each join.

exercises.title: Grain check: orders vs order lines
exercises.question: Before building an order report, an analyst wants to see what joining order_items does to the row count.
exercises.prompt: Return a single row with columns orders_rows (COUNT(*) of orders), joined_rows (COUNT(*) of orders INNER JOIN order_items on order_id) and distinct_orders_joined (number of distinct order_id values in that join).
hints: A scalar subquery (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) can sit in the SELECT list.
COUNT(*) counts joined rows; COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) counts orders that survived.
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_rows, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS distinct_orders_joined FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON ...
exercises.why: This three-number check (left rows, joined rows, distinct left keys) is the fastest way to catch both fan-out and silently dropped rows before they reach a dashboard.

recall.q: After an inner join, joined_rows > left rows and distinct keys < left rows. What two things happened?
recall.a: Fan-out (one-to-many repeated left rows) AND some left rows had no match and were dropped.

exercises.join_notes: Two effects at once: 60 orders become 150 joined rows (one per line — orders with up to 5 lines are repeated up to 5 times), yet only 59 distinct orders survive because order 60 (pending) has no items and the inner join drops it. Row count going UP does not mean nothing was lost.

exercises.title: Joined rows vs real order count per customer
exercises.question: A report counted 'orders per customer' after joining order lines and got numbers that look too high. Show the wrong and right count side by side.
exercises.prompt: For every customer who has at least one order (any status), join customers → orders (inner) → order_items (LEFT JOIN, so orders without lines stay). Return customer_id, name, joined_rows (COUNT(*) of the joined rows) and order_count (number of distinct orders).
hints: Chain: customers JOIN orders, then LEFT JOIN order_items.
COUNT(*) counts lines (the inflated number); COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) counts orders.
... GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name with COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
exercises.why: COUNT(*) after a one-to-many join counts the child grain, not the parent. Most 'why is this number too big' tickets are exactly this.

recall.q: After joining orders to order_items, what does COUNT(*) count?

exercises.join_notes: customers → orders gives 59 rows (order 31's customer 99 doesn't exist, and customers 18/19/20 have no orders, so 17 customers remain). → order_items fans that out to 149 rows: 148 lines of those 59 orders plus 1 NULL-item row for order 60, kept by the LEFT JOIN. Customer 1 shows 22 joined_rows for 9 orders; customer 9's order 60 still counts as an order. COUNT(*) is the line grain; COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) restores the order grain.

exercises.title: Fan-out through orders → items → returns
exercises.question: Customer service wants every order that had a return: how many lines it had, how many were returned and how much was refunded.
exercises.prompt: For each order with at least one returned line, return order_id, line_count (number of order_items lines in the order), returned_lines (number of returns) and total_refund (SUM of refund_amount).
hints: Returns hang off order lines (order_item_id), not off orders.
LEFT JOIN returns so non-returned lines still count in line_count; then filter groups with HAVING.
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON ... LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id GROUP BY o.order_id HAVING COUNT(r.return_id) > 0
exercises.why: Multi-hop joins are where grain gets lost. Knowing that returns are per *line* tells you the join to items is the one that fans out, and the join to returns doesn't.

recall.q: Why LEFT JOIN returns instead of INNER JOIN here?
recall.a: An inner join would drop non-returned lines, so line_count would only count returned lines.

exercises.join_notes: orders → order_items fans 59 orders with lines out to 150 rows. returns is one row per returned line (10 rows, all different order_item_id), so the LEFT JOIN to it is one-to-zero-or-one: still 150 rows, 140 with NULL return columns. Grouping by order and keeping groups with COUNT(r.return_id) > 0 leaves 10 orders, each with exactly 1 returned line. Order 38 has 4 lines, including the duplicate-looking line 150 — only line 96 was returned (96.9). With an inner join to returns, line_count would wrongly be 1 for every order.

exercises.title: Find duplicate-looking order lines
exercises.question: Finance suspects the order feed loaded some order lines twice. Which lines are exact business duplicates of an earlier line?
exercises.prompt: Return one row per duplicate: original_item_id (the smaller order_item_id), duplicate_item_id (the larger), order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price — for pairs of lines with the same order_id, product_id, quantity and unit_price.
hints: Self join order_items on all four business columns.
The surrogate key order_item_id differs between the duplicates — use it to avoid self-matches and mirrored pairs.
... ON b.order_id = a.order_id AND b.product_id = a.product_id AND b.quantity = a.quantity AND b.unit_price = a.unit_price AND b.order_item_id > a.order_item_id
exercises.why: Surrogate keys make every row 'unique', hiding double-loads. Duplicate detection must compare the business columns, not the id.

recall.q: Why doesn't the primary key protect you from duplicate order lines?
recall.a: The PK is a surrogate id generated per load; duplicates get new ids, so you must compare business columns.

exercises.join_notes: Of 150 lines, only 2 pairs match on all four business columns: line 149 duplicates line 21 (order 9, product 5, 1 × 279.99) and line 150 duplicates line 96 (order 38, product 9, 3 × 32.3). Result: 2 rows. Without the b.order_item_id > a.order_item_id condition you would get 150 self-matches plus 4 mirrored rows. Order 9 is cancelled, but order 38 is completed — its duplicate inflates gross revenue by 96.90.

exercises.title: Two one-to-many tables: the inflation
exercises.question: A dashboard joins customers to both orders and web_events in one query. How badly does that multiply rows?
exercises.prompt: Join customers → orders (inner, on customer_id) and customers → web_events (inner, on customer_id) in ONE query. Per customer return customer_id, joined_rows (COUNT(*)), order_count (distinct orders) and event_count (distinct web events).
hints: Both orders and web_events join to customers on customer_id — not to each other.
Compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) * COUNT(DISTINCT w.event_id).
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN web_events w ON w.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id
exercises.why: This is the 'chasm trap': two independent one-to-many branches joined together produce their cross product per parent. Every SUM on either side becomes wrong.

recall.q: A customer has 4 orders and 10 web events. How many rows after joining both?
recall.a: 40 — orders × events, because the two children are unrelated to each other.

exercises.join_notes: For every customer joined_rows = order_count × event_count: customer 7 has 8 orders × 17 events = 136 rows. In total 59 order rows and 217 identified events explode into 828 joined rows across 17 customers. The 8 anonymous events (customer_id NULL) and customers 18-20 (no orders, no events) never match. Any SUM over order lines in this shape would be multiplied by the event count — that is how customer 7's 1,305.28 became 22,189.76.

exercises.title: Fix it: pre-aggregate, then join
exercises.question: Build the correct customer scorecard: revenue and web activity for every customer.
exercises.prompt: Return all 20 customers with columns customer_id, name, gross_revenue and web_events. gross_revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the customer's valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), rounded to 2 decimals, 0 if none. web_events = number of web_events rows for the customer, 0 if none. Pre-aggregate each side to one row per customer before joining.
hints: Build two subqueries/CTEs, each GROUP BY customer_id: revenue from valid orders' items, and event counts.
Now both are one row per customer — LEFT JOIN them to customers so all 20 stay, and COALESCE the NULLs to 0.
WITH rev AS (... GROUP BY o.customer_id), ev AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS events FROM web_events GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT ... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN rev ... LEFT JOIN ev ...
exercises.why: Pre-aggregating to a common grain is THE fix for fan-out. It's how every well-built metrics layer joins facts that live at different grains.

recall.q: What is the fix for the 'two one-to-many tables' inflation?
recall.a: Aggregate each child to the parent's grain first, then join the one-row-per-key results.

exercises.join_notes: rev has 17 rows (16 real customers with a valid order + orphan customer 99 from order 31, which never matches a customer) and ev has 18 rows (17 customers + one NULL customer_id group for anonymous events, which matches nothing). Both are one row per customer, so the joins are one-to-zero-or-one: 20 rows in, 20 out. Customer 7 now shows the true 1305.28 with 17 events. Customers 16, 18, 19, 20 have no valid order → NULL gross → COALESCE to 0; 18-20 also have no events → 0.

exercises.title: Revenue with duplicate lines removed
exercises.question: Finance wants to know how much the duplicate order lines distort order totals.
exercises.prompt: For each order that contains duplicate-looking lines (same order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price), return order_id, order_status, raw_gross (SUM(quantity * unit_price) over all lines, rounded to 2) and deduped_gross (the same sum after keeping only one copy of each distinct (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price), rounded to 2).
hints: SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price collapses exact duplicates.
Aggregate raw lines and deduped lines separately per order_id, then join both to orders; keep orders where the raw line count is bigger.

WITH raw AS (... GROUP BY order_id), dedup AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(...) ... FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ...) GROUP BY order_id) SELECT ... FROM orders o JOIN raw ... JOIN dedup ... WHERE raw.lines > dedup.lines
exercises.why: DISTINCT over the business columns is a quick de-dup, but use it consciously: if a customer truly bought the same item twice on two lines, it would wrongly merge them.

recall.q: Why not just use SUM(DISTINCT quantity * unit_price)?
recall.a: It would also merge two genuinely different lines that happen to have the same amount — de-dup rows, not values.

exercises.join_notes: raw and dedup are both one row per order (59 orders with lines), so joining them to orders does not multiply anything. dedup has 148 distinct lines instead of 150; only orders 9 and 38 lose a line, so 2 rows come back. Order 9 (cancelled): 966.98 raw → 686.99 deduped. Order 38 (completed): 298.30 → 201.40 — the 96.90 gap is real over-statement of valid gross revenue.

worked_example.question: How many rows does each step of orders → order_items → returns produce?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o
          LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id) AS with_items_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o
          LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
          LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id) AS with_returns_rows;
worked_example.explanation: 60 orders fan out to 151 rows once items are attached (150 lines + 1 NULL row for order 60, which has no items). Adding returns keeps 151: each line has at most one return, so that join is one-to-zero-or-one and does not multiply.

recipe:
**Recipe: guard every join against fan-out**

1. **State the grain** of each table: "one row per ___". orders = one per order; order_items = one per
   order line; returns = one per returned line; web_events = one per event.
2. **Classify each join**: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many. Joining the "one" side to the "many"
   side repeats the "one" row once per match.
3. **Count before and after**: `SELECT COUNT(*)` of the left table, then of the join. If the count grew,
   every column from the "one" side is now repeated.
4. **Never SUM a repeated column.** If two one-to-many tables hang off the same parent
   (customer → orders and customer → web_events), joining both gives orders × events rows per customer.
5. **Fix by pre-aggregating** each child to the parent's grain *first*, then join one-to-one:

```sql
WITH rev AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(...) AS gross FROM ... GROUP BY customer_id),
     ev  AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*)  AS events FROM web_events GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT c.customer_id, COALESCE(rev.gross, 0), COALESCE(ev.events, 0)
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN ev  ON ev.customer_id  = c.customer_id;
```

**Duplicate detection:** group by the columns that *should* be unique and look for `COUNT(*) > 1`, or
self join rows with identical business columns but different ids.

`COUNT(DISTINCT key)` can rescue counts, but there is no safe `SUM(DISTINCT ...)` — two different lines
with the same amount would collapse. Pre-aggregate instead.
common_mistakes: Summing a parent-level number (order total, refund) after joining to a child table — it repeats once per child row.
Joining two independent one-to-many tables in one query (customer → orders and customer → events): rows = orders × events.
Checking only that the row count went up and assuming nothing was lost — an inner join can fan out AND drop rows at the same time.
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT …) to 'fix' inflation; it merges genuinely equal amounts.
Trusting the surrogate primary key to guarantee no duplicates — compare the business columns.
recall: What one row of a table represents, e.g. one row per order line.
Joining a 'one' row to a 'many' table: the one-side row repeats once per match.
What three numbers should you check around every join?
Left-table rows, joined rows, and distinct left keys in the joined result.
How do you safely combine two metrics from different child tables?
Pre-aggregate each to the shared parent grain, then join one-to-one.
